stances.claim: Under Article IV, Section 1 of the Constitution, children with at least one Filipino parent automatically inherit Filipino citizenship and are 'natural-born citizens' or 'citizens from birth without having to perform any act'; David v. SET (Sept 20, 2016) extends this to foundlings.
Natural-born citizens enjoy constitutionally exclusive rights (president, VP, senator, representative, SC justice) not extended to naturalized citizens.

RA 9225's two requirements -- renunciation under oath of foreign citizenship and oath of allegiance to the Philippines -- apply only to natural-born Filipinos who lost citizenship through naturalization, not to dual citizens at birth.

Per Gana-Carait v. Comelec (Aug 12, 2022, J Rosario), where a dual citizen at birth uses the CRBA process and a US passport, this is not naturalization -- the documentation merely confirms what was already true at birth.

Cordora v. Comelec (Feb 19, 2009, J Carpio) further establishes that even where a parent 'petitioned' the child for US citizenship, the petition is treated as a 'superfluity' because the child was already dual at birth.

About 1 in 10 Filipinos lives and works abroad, especially in the US; this Gana-Carait clarification provides legal comfort that they need not undergo the 'rather tedious process' under RA 9225 to retain Philippine citizenship.

notable_anecdotes: The hypothetical 'Maria' -- born 1991 in the Philippines to a Filipino father and American mother, listed in the CRBA, US passport bearer for extensive travel -- constructed as the prototypical FilAm whose situation is now legally settled.

The doctrinal pairing of Gana-Carait (2022, J Rosario) and Cordora (2009, J Carpio) -- newer ruling joined to older ruling -- modeling how CJ tracks the development of a doctrine across more than a decade.

The Cordora 'superfluity' move -- where a parent's positive petition under US law is judicially deemed legally redundant because the child was already dual at birth -- highlighted as a quintessentially Filipino-protective interpretation.
The 1-in-10-Filipinos-abroad statistic deployed not as anti-emigration commentary but as the demographic warrant for legal accommodation.
Foundlings expressly included via David v. SET (2016) -- a quiet doctrinal generosity that extends natural-born status without parental proof.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why most Filipino-Americans need not undertake the tedious renunciation-and-oath process under RA 9225 to retain Philippine citizenship. Article IV, Section 1 of the Constitution provides that children of Filipino parents automatically inherit Filipino citizenship as 'natural-born citizens' -- and David v. SET (Sept 20, 2016) extends this to foundlings. These citizens-from-birth enjoy constitutionally exclusive rights -- only they may run for President, Vice President, senator, or representative, or be appointed Supreme Court (or lower collegiate court) justice -- that naturalized citizens cannot claim. RA 9225's two requirements (renunciation under oath of foreign citizenship and an oath of allegiance to the Philippines) apply only to natural-born Filipinos who lost citizenship through naturalization, not to dual citizens at birth. Walking the reader through a 'simple question' (US-born children of Filipino parents running for senator) and a 'more complicated question' (the hypothetical Maria, born 1991 in the PH to a Filipino father and American mother, listed in the CRBA, US passport for extensive travel), he cites Gana-Carait v. Comelec (Aug 12, 2022, J Ricardo R. Rosario): the CRBA process recognizes US citizenship she already held at birth, not naturalization. The earlier Cordora v. Comelec (Feb 19, 2009, J Antonio T. Carpio) had already held that even an American parent's positive petition for US citizenship was a 'superfluity' because the child was already dual at birth. Roughly one in ten Filipinos lives and works abroad -- most of them, CJ concludes, are recognized by the Philippines (not necessarily by the US) as dual citizens 'without the need to go through the rather tedious process under RA 9225.'
